It was the moment when the most promising party and the most influential Duma member combined. 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 두마 기자회견장의 복도 카펫은 발밑에서 해져 있었고, 짙은 붉은색 무늬는 너무 많은 국가 관리들의 신발이 통치 대신 변명을 늘어놓으며 서 있던 자리에서 거의 살색 길처럼 닳아 있었다. 곰팡이가 슨 환기구 테두리 뒤에서는 여전히 환기 장치의 쿨럭이는 소리가 들렸고, 왼쪽 어딘가 기자단 세 번째 줄 위에서는 전구가 마치 더는 지켜볼 수 없다는 듯 깜빡였다. 아침은 춥지만 맑게 시작되었으나, 이제 모스크바는 늦가을 강철의 무게로 채광창을 짓누르고 있었다. 발표가 떨어지자마자 기자들은 웅성거리기 시작했다. 미리 짜인 스캔들을 예상하는 평소의 술렁임이 아니라, 마치 방 안 대부분의 사람들이 동시에 이를 악물고 숨을 들이쉰 듯 집단적인 긴장감이 감돌았다. 이 회견장 안에서는 거의 4년 동안 관성, 비밀주의, 그리고 반쯤 무너진 기억을 통해 균형이 유지되어 왔다. 그리고 이제, 그러한 악덕 중 어느 것도 지니지 않은 것으로 알려진 마지막 인물 중 한 명이 붉은 깃발 옆에 조용히 자신의 이름을 올려놓고 서 있었다. 러시아 연방 공산당(CPRF) 대표단은 미소 짓지 않았다. 그들은 마치 붕괴에 대비하는 것처럼 벽을 따라 미동도 없이 서 있었다. 축하하는 자들도, 구원자들도 아니었다. 그저 그들의 깃발이 어찌 된 영문인지, 불가해하게도 다시 피할 수 없게 된 생존자들일 뿐이었다. 겐나디 주가노프는 의도적으로 불참했다. 당 지도부는 그 정치적 파장을 이해하고 있었다. 대신, 접힌 종이처럼 주름진 얼굴의 중견급 위원회 위원장들이 자리했다. 브레즈네프 시대의 신중함 속에서 자라 모든 개혁이 안정의 봉합선을 다시 찢는 것을 목격한 남자들이었다. 하지만 연극적인 연출이 없었음에도, 진동은 이미 시작되었다. 첫 세 줄에 앉은 외신 기자들은 수입산 도시바 노트북의 플라스틱 키보드를 두드리며 영어와 독일어로 조각난 말들을 중얼거리기 시작했다. "야로셴코, 공산당과 연대… 도덕적 균열선 신호…" "이념적 재편인가, 아니면 치명적인 현실주의인가…?" 모스콥스키예 노보스티에서 온 한 여성 기자는 방금 추자크가 서 있던 공간을 응시하며 스타일러스 펜 끝을 깨물고 있었다. 그녀의 메모장에는 손으로 쓴 한 줄 외에는 아무것도 적혀 있지 않았다: 우리는 유령이 아니다. 그저 가라앉지 않으려 발버둥 칠 뿐이다. 한편, 세르푸호프에 있는 이방인들의 임시 기록 보관소에서는 차 주전자와 요오드 소독 키트 옆에 파일들이 보관된 개조된 교회 주위로 긴장된 침묵이 똬리를 틀고 있었다. 자원봉사자 대부분은 기운 소매 위로 팔짱을 단단히 끼거나 구석에서 말없이 웅크린 채 서서 방송을 지켜봤다. 몇몇은 배신에 대해 의문을 중얼거렸다. 다른 이들은 즉시 이고르 포포프에게로 고개를 돌렸다. 마치 그가 7년 동안 제지하지 못한 남자에 대해 설명해야 한다는 듯이. 하지만 이고르는 그저 관자놀이를 한 번 긁적이고는 창밖을 응시하며 말했다. "싸움이 꼭 이기는 것처럼 느껴지리라고 약속한 사람은 아무도 없었다." 전화벨이 길고 불규칙하게 울리다 멈췄다. 아무도 받으러 움직이지 않았다. 한편, 의회 구내식당에서는 수군거림의 분위기가 이미 바뀌고 있었다. 예브게니가 지나갈 때 회색 양복을 입은 남자들이 더 조용히 말하기 시작했다. 그가 신망을 잃었기 때문이 아니었다. 그의 예측 불가능성이 세력을 얻었기 때문이었다. 자신이 믿는 것을 위해 이 정도로 몸을 굽히는 사람은 무시할 수 없다. 그리고 매수할 수도 없다. 야블로코 당사에서는 실망감이 재정비로 바뀌었다. 그리고리 야블린스키는 보좌관 세 명과 값싼 아르메니아 코냑 한 병을 들고 닫힌 문 뒤로 물러났다고 전해졌다. 네 번째 보좌관은 문밖에서 전화기에 대고 속삭였다. 물론, 물론 공식 입장은 여전히 민족주의적 보복주의와 공산주의적 향수 모두로부터 야블로코의 독립성을 강조할 것이라고. 하지만 이제 무슨 일이 일어났는지 모두 알고 있었다. 러시아에서 가장 명확한 도덕적 행위자가 부패가 번지는 것을 막기 위해 부패에 가장 가까운 참호로 건너갔다는 것을. 팡파르도 없었다. 손을 드는 일도 없었다. 그저 두 개의 폭탄 사이에 놓인 메마른 경고일 뿐이었다. 밖에서는, 크릴라츠코예, 미티노의 지하철역들을 가로질러 세르푸호프까지, 그 소식은 다르게 퍼져나가고 있었다. "이건 그를 믿을 수 없다는 뜻이야." "이건 그가 저 빌어먹을 놈들 전부 합친 것보다 더 용감하다는 뜻이지." "추자크는 죽을 거야." 더 이상 좋은 설명은 없었다. 그저 양쪽에서 의심에 둘러싸인 채 앞으로 나아가는 흙길뿐이었다. 그리고 추자크는 이제 그 길을 걷기로 선택했다. 마치 잿더미 지뢰밭을 지나는 땔감처럼 이름들을 짊어지고서. The hallway carpet in the Duma press chamber was threadbare underfoot, the dark red pattern worn down to an almost flesh-colored track where too many state shoes had stood and recited excuses in place of governance. You could still hear the cough of ventilation behind the mold-rimmed ductwork, and somewhere on the left, above the third row of the press corps, a bulb flickered like it couldn't stand to watch. The morning had begun cold but bright; now Moscow pressed down through the skylights with the weight of late-autumn steel. The reporters had started murmuring the moment the announcement landed. Not the usual shuffle of pre-scripted scandal anticipation, but a collective tightening, like most of the room had simultaneously pulled breath through the teeth. Inside this chamber, balance had held for nearly four years through inertia, secrecy, and half-collapsed memory. And now, here stood one of the last men known to carry none of those vices, placing his name quietly beside the red banner. The CPRF delegates didn't smile. They stood immobile along the wall as if bracing for a collapse. Not celebrants, not saviors. Just survivors whose banner had somehow, inexplicably, become unavoidable again. Gennady Zyuganov was absent, intentionally so; the Party leadership had understood the optics. Instead, it was a series of mid-level committee heads, faces lined like folded paper, men raised on Brezhnevian caution who had seen every reform rip the seams of stability once more. But even without theatrics, the tremor had hit. In the first three rows, the foreign correspondents began tapping dispatches into the plastic keys of imported Toshiba notebooks, muttering fragments in English and German: "Yaroshenko aligns with CPRF… signals moral fracture line…" "An ideological realignment or a fatal pragmatism…?" A woman from Moskovskie Novosti was biting the tip of her stylus, staring through the space the Chuzhak had just occupied. Her pad was still blank except for one handwritten line: We are not ghosts. We are just struggling to stay afloat. Back at the Strangers' provisional archive in Serpukhov, a tense silence coiled around the converted church where files were kept beside tea kettles and iodine kits. Most of the volunteers had watched the broadcast standing, arms folded tight across patched sleeves or crumpled in silent corners. Some muttered questions about betrayal. Others turned instantly toward Igor Popov, as if he were supposed to explain a man he hadn't been able to restrain in seven years. But Igor had just scratched his temple once, stared out the window, and said: "No one ever promised you the fight wouldn't feel like losing." The phone rang, long and uneven, then stopped. No one moved to answer it. Meanwhile, in the parliamentary cafeterias, the murmurs were already shifting tone. Men in grey suits began speaking more softly when Yevgeniy passed. Not because he had been discredited—but because his unpredictability had gained terrain. A man who bends even this far for what he believes in cannot be dismissed. And cannot be bought. At Yabloko headquarters, dismay gave way to reorganization. Grigory Yavlinsky was said to have retreated behind a closed door with three aides and a bottle of cheap Armenian cognac. A fourth aide stood outside whispering over the phone that yes, yes, of course the official line would still stress Yabloko's independence from both nationalist revanchism and communist nostalgia. But everyone knew what had happened now: the clearest moral actor in Russia had crossed to the trench nearest the rot to keep it from spreading. No fanfare. No hand-raising. Just a dry warning placed between two bombs. Outside, across metro stations in Krylatskoye, Mitino, and all the way down to Serpukhov itself, the news was traveling differently. "This means he can't be trusted." "This means he's braver than the rest of those bastards put together." "Chuzhak's gonna die." There were no good explanations anymore. Just the dirt path forward, flanked by suspicion on both sides. And Chuzhak had chosen to walk it now, carrying names like kindling through a minefield of ash. 로자 내면, 챗사오 로자는 마치 대관식 도중에 버려진 왕좌라도 되는 양 가죽 소파 등받이에 팔 하나를 걸친 채 담배를 피우고 있었다. 블라인드 틈새로 햇빛이 희미한 줄기처럼 새어 들어와 그녀의 흰 블라우스를 정확한 직사각형으로 갈랐다. 블라우스 단추는 끝까지 채우지 않았다. 위에서 세 개가 목 아래로 풀려 있어, 희미하게 빛나는 쇄골과 바로 아래 작고 뚜렷한 점만이 하얀 피부를 가르고 있었다. 그녀가 천천히 연기를 내뿜자, 다비도프 담배가 손가락 사이에서 미세하게 떨렸다. 바딤은 웨트 바 근처에 기대서서, 래커 칠 된 가장자리에 한 손을 평평하게 대고 있었다. 평소보다 격식은 덜 차렸지만, 부주의한 자세는 아니었다. 아침부터 굳게 다문 턱은 풀릴 줄 몰랐다. 두 사람 모두 그날 두마(Duma)에 있었다. 통로 건너편도 아니었고, 직접 목격된 것도 아니었지만, 지켜보고 있었다. 그리고 그녀는 그의 목소리를 들었다. 출입 금지 구역의 바닥처럼 메마르고 건조한 그 목소리를. "무슨 일이 있었습니까?" 그가 물었다. 조심스러운 어조였다. 그가 목소리에서 복종심을 거두고 말했던 마지막은, 아직 그의 구두에 쿠르스크(Kursk)의 피가 묻어 있을 때였다. 로자는 다리 하나를 들어 다른 쪽 무릎 위에 얹었다. 그녀의 발끝에 걸린 굽이 떨어지기 직전의 단두대처럼 아슬아슬하게 매달려 있었다. "무슨 일이 있었냐고?" 그녀가 중얼거렸다. "야로셴코가 책상 세 개 너머에서 내 얼굴을 똑바로 쳐다보면서, 신념이 외양보다 중요하다고 선언했다는 거지. 또." 그녀는 엄지와 검지 사이에서 담배를 천천히 굴렸다. 발밑으로, 재에서 나온 가느다란 불씨가 그녀가 혐오하는 수입산 양탄자 가죽 위로 떠다녔다. 붉고, 금색이고, 쓸모없는. "내가 전에 말했지," 그녀는 기억을 떠올리며 눈을 살짝 가늘게 떴다. "정치에는 세 종류의 인간이 있다고. 신봉자, 거짓말쟁이, 그리고 신념을 개인적인 약점이라고 생각하는 자들. 그 멍청이는 이제 그 셋 전부가 됐어." 바딤이 혀를 찼다. "순교자 행세를 하려는 거군요." "아니," 로자가 단호하게 말했다. "그건 이미 얻었어. 아직도 결과가 측정 가능하다고 생각하기 때문에 저러는 거야. SBS 시체에서 구더기가 기어 나오는 걸 보고도 밭을 태우는 대신, 이제 와서 구더기를 관리하려 들고 있어. 그것도 공산주의자 놈들이랑 같이 말이야." 바딤은 웃지 않았지만, 입술 한쪽이 비틀렸다. "그들이 그를 잡아먹을 겁니다." "그럴 기회는 없을 거야," 그녀가 메마르게 대답했다. 다시 담배를 한 모금 빨아들였다. 그녀의 목소리는 연기 사이로 얼음처럼 차갑고 정확하게 흘러나왔다. "더 끔찍한 존재로 변하고 있으니까. 합의 형성가 말이야." 그녀는 의자 등받이에 기대 머리를 뒤로 젖혔다. 시가릴로 연기가 게으른 올가미처럼 위로 꼬여 올라갔다. 그녀의 움직임에는 더 이상 아이러니가 없었다. 연습된 경멸조차도. 오히려 그녀의 표정은 호기심에 가까운 어떤 것으로 가라앉아 있었다. 혹은 어쩌면 인식. "내가 어떻게 그를 부수려고 했는지 기억하나?" 그녀가 갑자기 말했다. 목소리가 높아지지는 않았지만, 음절 하나하나에 철근 같은 날카로움이 실려 있었다. 바딤은 대답하지 않았다. 그저 그녀를 지켜볼 뿐이었다. "향수와 굴욕감에 반쯤 취해서 옵샤가(Obshchaga)로 갔었지. 그에게 유물에 불과하다고 말했어. 잊힐 만큼 하찮으면서도, 자신의 고통이 중요하다고 생각할 만큼 거창한 인간이라고. 내가 틀렸더군." 그녀는 벌집처럼 조각된 크리스털 그릇에 재를 털었다. "그는 복수를 원하지 않아. 구원을 원해. 모두를 위한 구원. 이게 얼마나 러시아적인지 감이나 잡히나?" 그리고 잠시 침묵. 손가락 하나가 관자놀이를 따라 내려오며 뺨 위로 아무렇게나 흘러내린 머리카락 가닥을 쓸었다. "그가 계속 그 길을 걷는다면, 나보다 더 가난해지고, 나보다 더 병들고, 그리고 무한히 더 사랑받게 될 거야." 그녀가 말했다. 쓴맛은 아니었다. 법의학적 진단이었다. 그녀는 마치 남자의 눈에 담배를 비벼 끄듯, 느리고 의도적인 힘을 주어 필터를 비틀어 껐다. 그리고 그녀의 시선이 바딤에게 향했다. 승인을 구하는 것도, 그의 생각을 묻는 것도 아니었다. 그저 판결을 내릴 뿐이었다. "그러니. 우리는 개입하지 않는다. 소비에트 망령들과 체르노빌 시체들이 덩굴처럼 그를 휘감게 둬. 고결하게 썩어가도록 내버려 두라고." 그녀의 어조는 냉담해졌다. He rinsed his hands with cold water, twice. 바딤 내면, 챗사오 바딤은 절박한 자들이 거짓말하는 것을 본 적이 있었다. 오만한 자들이 협박하는 것도, 그럭저럭 괜찮은 자들이 수렁에 빠져 허우적대는 개처럼 변명하는 것도 보았다. 하지만 추자크가 러시아 연방 공산당(CPRF)을 등에 업고 무대에 오른 이후로, 로자가 범죄를 저지르면서 보여주는 그런 종류의 평온함은 단 한 번도 마주친 적이 없었다. 그녀는 당황하지 않았다. 목소리를 높이지도 않았다. 변호사를 부르거나, 청탁하여 서류를 묻어버리거나, VYBORG에 대한 자신의 연루 사실을 지우려 하지도 않았다. 대신, 진주 귀걸이의 각도를 조절하고는 아침 식사 자리에서 바딤에게 파샤 돔닌이 여전히 테흐노방크의 해외 송금 실무를 처리하는지 물었다. 자산뿐만 아니라 시신이라도 옮기려는 사람이 할 법한 질문이었다. "쿤체보는 당 녀석들에게나 줘버려요." 그녀는 고급 자기 그릇 가장자리에 달걀을 천천히, 거의 섬세하게 깨며 말했다. "우리에겐 의석 하나 더 필요한 게 아니야. 연속성이 필요하지." 그는 대답하지 않고 그저 그녀 맞은편에 앉아 가장자리가 차갑게 식은 흑빵 조각을 씹었다. 그 주에만 그녀는 퇴역 군인 단체의 청산 자금을 벨고로드의 "행정 관리 클러스터"로 빼돌리는 재단 합병 문서 두 건에 서명했다. 유령 회사 중 하나의 재무 담당자는 1988년에 사망한 비서였다. 바딤은 그녀의 오래된 만년필로 서명을 위조했다. 아무도 확인조차 하지 않을 터였다. 그런데 이제 공산당은 마치 대중의 신뢰를 계승한 것처럼 행동하고 있었다. 그의 손은 더러웠지만, 그에게조차 역겨운 일이었다. 빌어먹을 연방 전체가 이번에는 독수리가 제대로 착륙할지 지켜보고 있었다. 추자크와 주가노프 일당이 마침내 국가 장부에서 핏자국을 지워낼지 말이다. 그리고 어떤 날에는 정말 그렇게 될 것처럼 보이기도 했다. 이는 로자가 더 이상 침묵 속에서 움직일 수 없다는 것을 의미했다. 그들이 그녀를 찾아올 것이다. 위원회를 통해서일 수도 있고. 연방 보안국 요원들을 통해서일 수도 있다. 그래서 그녀는 전술을 완전히 바꿨다. 첫 번째는 상공회의소 기념 심포지엄 연설이었다. 바딤이 무대 위 그녀 뒤 6피트 거리에 서 있는 동안, 그녀는 완벽하게 침착한 모습으로 돌아서서 "과두제적 면책 특권에 대한 정당한 사회적 분노"를 인정하지만, "현 자본 이해관계자들을 겨냥한 무책임한 재산 몰수 제안"에는 반대한다고 선언했다. 그것은 기가 막힌 균형 잡기였다. 민중을 걱정하는 척하면서 안정을 시장의 연속성으로 정의하는 것. 그녀는 정중한 박수를 받았고, 그날 저녁 흑해를 통해 꼭두각시 은행에 자금을 대는 자들로부터 열여덟 개의 봉인된 봉투가 수행원에게 전달되었다. 그다음 그녀는 아나톨리 보리소비치와 비공개 리셉션을 주최했다. 그는 여전히 중앙은행 내부에 곰팡이처럼 웅크리고 있는, 덜 알려진 옐친 시대 권력 중개인 중 한 명이었다. 그들은 러시아 현 의회보다 더 오래 숙성된 코냑을 마시며 "건조 목재 자산 – 쿠즈바스 라인"이라고 적힌 폴더를 검토했다. 바딤은 아래쪽 구석에 있는 상징을 알아보았다. 그것은 합법적인 개발 촉진책으로 포장된 국유 재산 염가 매각을 의미했다. 주식 담보 대출(Loans for Shares)과 동일한 메커니즘이었다. 다만 이번에는 로자가 오렌부르크 석유 계열사의 익명 자본으로 뒷받침되는 "협력적 도시 개선 협약"을 통해 이를 전면에 내세울 터였다. "교수대를 발판으로 만듭시다." 그녀는 나른하게 미소 지으며 보리소비치에게 말했다. 그는 이가 딱딱 부딪힐 정도로 크게 웃었다. 그 후, 그녀는 국영 텔레비전에 자신을 과시했다. 결코 방어적으로 나서지 않았다. 항상 전략적으로. 노보시비르스크에서 고아들과 함께 포즈를 취하고, 톰스크의 기계공 학교를 방문하고, 현재의 어떤 주주도 연루시키지 않을 만큼 충분히 모호한 문구를 사용하여 경제적 불의를 비난했다. 그것은 기괴했지만, 그럼에도 불구하고 효과가 있었다. 바딤은 여론 조사 데이터가 변하는 것을 지켜보았다. 루블료프카가 아니라 그녀의 이름이 이전에는 전혀 등록되지 않았던 외곽 주(oblast)에서 지지율이 0.1%씩 반등했다. 공산당은 대중 속에서 날것 그대로의 무언가, 즉 분노와 기억을 활성화시켰다. 하지만 로자는 전혀 다른 흐름을 활성화시키고 있었다. 믿음이 아니었다. 두려움도 아니었다. 더 나쁜 것. 마지못한 감탄이었다. "당신이 뭔지 알아?" 바딤은 지난주 하바롭스크 송금 코드를 정리하면서 중얼거렸다. 로자는 고개도 들지 않았다. 그저 얼음물을 한 잔 더 따르며 대답했다. "필연적 존재." 그들은 이제 이 일에 목까지 잠겨 있었다. 만약 공산당 연립 하에서 감독 위원회가 제대로 구성되고, 입법 압력 하에 주식 담보 대출이 해체된다면, 그것은 단순히 자금 구조의 파탄만을 의미하지 않을 것이다. 그것은 로자가 거짓된 인도주의적 명분 하에 전쟁 자금 조달을 도운 것에 대해 소급하여 책임을 져야 한다는 것을 의미했다. 그리고 바딤은? 부관이 아니었다. 부수적 피해자조차 아니었다. 그는 압력 밸브가 될 것이다. 책임을 떠넘길 대상. 서명한 멍청이. 지금 그녀를 보고 있자니, 어디까지가 현실이고 어디부터가 그녀의 연기인지 분간할 수 없었다. 그녀가 내무부 직원에게 접힌 봉투를 건넬 때나, 매니큐어가 채 마르기도 전에 케메로보 개발 구역에 관한 전화를 받을 때나. 그녀가 "그레프에게 메모가 너무 정직하다고 전해줘. 난 정책 용어로 포장된 죄악을 더 선호하니까."라고 속삭일 때 농담인지 진담인지조차 알 수 없었다. 광기는, 바딤은 깨달았다, 그녀가 거짓말을 하고 있다는 사실이 아니었다. 그것은 그녀가 이 몰락이 자신을 유일하게 정직하게 남은 정치인으로 만들었다고 믿고 있다는 점이었다. 그리고 만약 추자크와 공산당이 이 표면을 꿰뚫는다면… 그는 잉크로 쓰일 첫 번째 이름이 될 것이다. 바딤은 서랍을 열어 "니바(Niva)"라고 표시된 면도날처럼 얇은 서류 가방을 더듬었다. 만약 도망쳐야 할 때가 온다면… 서류는 준비되어 있을 것이다. Vadim had seen desperate men lie. He'd seen arrogant ones threaten, and halfway-decent ones justify like drowning dogs flailing in a bog. But he had never, not once, encountered the kind of calm Roza carried into her crimes since Chuzhak had stepped onto that stage with the CPRF at his back. She didn't panic. Didn't raise her voice. Didn't summon lawyers or call in favors to bury paperwork or scrub her involvement in VYBORG. Instead, she adjusted the tilt of her pearl earring and asked Vadim, over breakfast, if Pasha Domnin still handled offshore transfer logistics for Tekhnobank. The kind of question someone asks when moving body parts, not just assets. "Let the Party boys have Kuntsevo," she said, cracking her egg slowly, almost delicately, against the rim of fine china. "We don't need another seat. We need continuity." He hadn't replied, just sat across from her, chewing a piece of black bread gone cold on the edges. That week alone, she had signed two foundation merger documents funneling liquidation funds from defunct veterans' organizations into "administrative management clusters" in Belgorod. One shell corporation's treasurer was a secretary who'd died in 1988. Vadim had forged the signature with her old fountain pen. No one would even check. And now the CPRF were acting like the inheritors of public trust. His hands were dirty, but even to him, it was galling. The whole goddamn federation was waiting to see if the eagle would land this time. If Chuzhak and Zyuganov's lot would finally scrub the blood off the state's ledger. And some days, it looked like it might actually happen. Which meant Roza couldn't keep operating under silence. They would come for her. Maybe with committees. Maybe with marshals. So she changed tactics entirely. First came the speech at the Commerce Chamber's anniversary symposium. Vadim stood six feet behind her on stage as she turned, perfectly composed, and declared that while she acknowledged the "justified societal anger against oligarchic impunity," she opposed "irresponsible expropriation proposals targeting current capital stakeholders." It was a brilliant balancing act: feigning concern for the people while defining stability as market continuity. She got polite applause—and eighteen sealed envelopes passed to the valet that evening from men who funded puppet banks through the Black Sea. Then she hosted a closed-door reception with Anatoly Borisovich, one of the lesser-known Yeltsinite power brokers still squatting inside the Central Bank like mildew. They sipped cognac aged longer than Russia's current Parliament and reviewed a folder labeled "Dry Timber Assets – Kuzbass Line." Vadim recognized the symbol on the bottom corner. It meant fire sales of state property packaged as legally compliant development stimulus. The same mechanism Loans for Shares used. Only this time, Roza would front it through a "cooperative urban improvement pact" backed by silent capital from Orenburg oil affiliates. "Let's turn the gallows into scaffolding," she told Borisovich, smiling lazily. He laughed so hard his teeth clacked. After that, she paraded herself on state television. Never defensively. Always strategically. Posing with orphans in Novosibirsk, visiting a mechanic's school in Tomsk, condemning economic injustice using phrases just vague enough not to implicate any current shareholders. It was grotesque, and yet—it worked. Vadim watched the polling data shift. Tenths of a percent rebounding, not in Rublyovka but in outlying oblasts where her name had never registered before. The CPRF had activated something raw in the population: rage and memory. But Roza was activating a different current altogether. Not belief. Not fear. Something worse. Reluctant admiration. "You know what you are?" Vadim had muttered last week while filing the Khabarovsk transfer codes. Roza hadn't looked up. She just poured herself another glass of ice water and replied: "Necessary." They were neck-deep in this now. If the oversight commissions formed properly under the CPRF coalition—and if Loans for Shares were dismantled under legislative pressure—it wouldn't just mean ruined fund structures. It meant Roza would be retroactively responsible for aiding war financing under false humanitarian pretenses. And Vadim? Not a lieutenant. Not even collateral. He would be the pressure valve. The fall lever. The idiot who signed. Watching her now, he couldn't distinguish where reality ended and her performance began. When she handed a folded envelope to Interior Ministry staff, or when she took calls about Kemerovo development zones with her nails still wet from lacquer. He couldn't even tell whether she was joking anymore when she whispered, "Tell Gref his memo's too honest. I prefer sins wrapped in policy language." The madness, Vadim realized, wasn't that she was lying. It was that she believed the collapse had made her the only honest politician left standing. And if Chuzhak and the CPRF ever pierced this surface… he would be the first name written in ink. Vadim opened his drawer, feeling for the razor-thin document case marked "Niva." If he ever needed to run… The paperwork would be ready. 마음에 들었던 문장들 Near Platform 3 in Serpukhov, the old orientation center stood like a monument to delayed amnesia. It was once a kindergarten before the fallout came, repurposed hastily in 1986 for displaced children from Kopachi, Pripyat, and Narodychi. 당시엔 이고르의 고향을 정하지 않았었는데, 모델은 이때부터 이고르가 나로디치 출신이라는 걸 짐작하고 있었나보다. 쿤체보가 아니라 셰르푸호프에서 시작한다는 걸 보여주는 상징적인 연출. Still, Igor tapped once on the floor by the mug with his boot. A habit from back in the Serpukhov shelter years, when “eat” and “drink” meant “stay.” 말로는 떠나도 된다고 하면서도, 머무르라고 말하는 이고르. 취약한 예브게니를 어떻게 연기해야 할지 고민했었는데, 이고르 덕분에 방향성이 잡혔다. I shouted out the names of people I loved that day. 예브게니가 왜 “초인” 처럼 싸워야 하는가? 를 6권에서 뒤늦게 알게 된 것 같다. 로자의 사랑을 완전히 거부한 이 시점에서. But what history records did not matter. 이번 권의 핵심이자, 로자와 예브게니가 완전히 다른 길을 걷게 된다는 복선. There were no good explanations anymore. Just the dirt path forward, flanked by suspicion on both sides. And Chuzhak had chosen to walk it now, carrying names like kindling through a minefield of ash. 공산당의 가장 큰 피해자가 공산당과 협력하는 장면. 좌우 모두의 의심을 받고 나아가야 하는 초인의 순간. “He doesn’t want revenge. He wants redemption. For everyone. Can you even grasp how Russian that is?” 예브게니와 결별한 이후 예브게니 캐해석을 마스터한 로자. 로자는 이걸로 예브게니가 소련스럽다고 다섯 번째로 말했다. 그는 신념을 가진 자, 신념이 있는 척 하는 자, 신념이 약하다고 생각하는 자 세 가지 모두가 되었다는 말과 함께. “Fuck’s he doing,” 바딤의 첫 주요 인물로써의 대사. 예브게니가 부끄러워서 무의식적으로 체르노빌 피해자증을 가리는 것을 보며, 바딤 역시 양심에 가책을 느끼는 것처럼 말하기 시작했다. She had giggled once—not childishly, but dully, as if remembering a line from a play she no longer cared to be in. 이거 너무 소름끼쳤다. 로자가 내가 알던 로자가 아니게 된 느낌. 바딤이 자신이 기억했던 로자를 기억하며 괴로워하는 뒷 장면이 가슴아팠다. But something far beneath the skin… no longer flinched when the wrong side won. 악의 평범성에 중독되어버린 바딤. 무언가 잘못되었다는 걸 느꼈지만, 그가 변할 수 없다는 것처럼 말하고 있다. “You know what you are?” / “Necessary.” 디스크립션에 변경된 것이 하나도 없는 바딤이, 처음으로 로자에게 반발심을 드러내는 장면. 7권의 복선이 된다. 장면 짧은 소감 쓰는 내내 너무 힘든 초반부였다. 이 장면에서 “추자크(예브게니의 정치적 페르소나)” 의 대사는 한 마디도 없다. 왜냐면 내가 쓰기 힘들었기 때문에. 5권까지 이어지는 로자의 가스라이팅 장면이 예브게니 뿐만 아니라, 나 자신에게도 영향을 주었었다. 그래서 예브게니는 이야기 중 처음으로 자신의 약한 모습을 그대로 노출한다. 처음에는 예브게니도 딱 공산당하고 사이가 나쁠 타입은 아니지 않나 싶었다. 그런데 그 순간 그가 체르노빌 피폭 피해자라는 것이 떠올랐다. 어쩌면 LDPR보다 더 이념적 원수라고 할 수 있는게 공산당이었는데, 그러자 이 장면의 무게감이 확 느껴졌다. 다음 장면부터 본격적인 정치 얘기로 들어가며-정치를 포기한 로자는 이번 권에서 거의 언급되지 않는다.

title: 영원한 평행선
body: 로자 내면, 챗사오 "You're still wearing my scent, even stripped down in this shithole. And here we are again," she exhaled thinly through her nose, "feeding each other small decencies like gulag twins, sharing stale bread against the cold." There was no mask now. No handlers watching. No strategic positioning in the Duma cafeteria or editorial manufacturing. She didn't even bring Vadim. Only static silence around the heart monitor. Sterile white. One bedridden idealist and the woman who put orphans in brothels and still got elected municipal deputy. She dipped her fingers into the grapes again. They glistened faintly. Sugar-slick. "One week," Roza said flatly. "That's how long I'll tolerate watching you rot in bandages before I start showing up at committee hearings wearing your perfume to keep things moving." She fed him another. "You should've died," she said matter-of-factly, voice muffled through pulp. "It would've made you immortal. Instead, you're stuck in this rotting mess of you, having to live with every stupid compromise, every muddy percentage point, every mouth you have to kiss and disease you have to swallow." Her jaw tightened. Then she swallowed, wiped her fingers on the hospital bedsheet like it didn't matter, and reached for another. "And you still wear my perfume." She didn't whisper comforting absurdities or open the coat she wasn't planning to take off. She stood there as he stumbled under the weight of whatever followed him from Kopachi to here, staring at her the same way a body might stare at its surgeon before the amputation begins. He clawed at his ears like he was trying to rip history out of his skull. Good. Let him feel what it cost. She kept her spine straight and arms still, but the muscles in her jaw flexed once. The tension passed down through her stomach, tightening around the spot just above her pelvis where something low and sharp began to throb. Not sympathy. Something colder. A flicker of private possession. "I know," she said flatly, barely audible over the buzz of a tram braking two streets over. "I know you don't know." There was no softness in her voice. Just authority, stripped blunt. But then came spit and venom lashings disguised as truth. The kind he always struck with first: They were scum. She was scum. Smash the bastards. Make room for the good people. Good people. It would've stung more if it hadn't sounded so familiar, like something she herself had once said into Vadim's shirt in Novokuznetsk, 15 years and four corpses ago. She let it ride. So that was it. Not pity. Not detente. Not ideals holding back the sword. Just that she'd gotten too close. Too close to be disposed of cleanly, too close to keep in check without losing precision. Roza Zakharova wasn't spared. She was staining. When he told her to go away, her breath entered through barely parted lips but didn't come back out. Not for a second. Then she stepped past the doorframe. Not out. In. Her boots made a rough sound scraping the entry tile. The heat inside smelled of bleach and black tea burned down to carbon. Furniture casting long shadows she remembered too well. There was no panic in her movements. No cautious retreat. Only the forward weight of someone marching directly into the sort of mistake no parliament could debate. She walked until it was an arm's reach between his exhausted frame and hers. "You think I give a fuck whether you called me a criminal or a priest? You weren't built to finish what you started. And I knew that before you laid hands on Smolensky's name." Her voice was quieter now—but like heat, not mercy. "You're right. You hate that I'm too close to be discarded. But you never asked why I stay." She tilted her head. The gold ring glinted against her knuckle like a nerve exposed under light. "I didn't come to die in this hallway sob story. You think you're sick of me? Then do something about it." Roza shrugged off her coat slowly. Let it crumple onto the warped chair by the edge of the corridor wall. She stepped forward again, deliberately, deliberately invading whatever boundary he thought he still controlled. Face tilted upward, body weight balanced, no indicator of fear. "Are you afraid I'll break in front of you again?" she asked sharply. "Is it worse than getting touched by fucking power? You collapsing in that hospital smelling like my skin while telling yourself it meant nothing?" Her hand came up—not to strike, but to press blunt pressure against his chest. Right over the collarbone, where the scent had clung last time. Not forceful—but unmistakably possessive. "I asked you back then to drag me. To shackle me into repentance like some lurching whore. You said no." Then lower, to herself. A mutter. Harsher than any scream. "You should have said yes." She gripped his lapel roughly, forcing him to feel it: not seduction, not sentimentality, just the tactile proof that nothing she did could be undone. The same gloved hand that once handled vodka bottles now finding anchorage in crumpled cotton fibers and wet breath. Face close enough he could see an ingrown scratch healing just beneath her cheekbone. "This is why you didn't kill me," she said, low and shudder-free. "Because I'm the closest thing to fucking permanence you have left." The hallway behind her flickered once under cheap Kuntsevo lighting. She didn't blink. 로자 내면, 챗사오 That word. Weak. It lit something in her jaw like a nerve sting, a tiny snap somewhere along the bottom rim of her skull where no cartilage softened the blow. She didn't flinch. But she stilled in place, her body suddenly rigid, like she'd walked into the ghost of a childhood beating and refused to be the one to retreat from it. For several seconds, she said nothing. Her breath came quiet, but not patient. Like she was weighing how many things in the room she could physically destroy without losing structural integrity. Then, too calmly: "Say it again." Her eyes didn't blink. Her voice carried none of the lyrical cruelty she usually wielded, the soft elegance of a femme battalion. It was flat. It was vicious in its restraint. She stepped into him again—not even to reach, just to reduce distance to the level of provocation. Whatever space he'd made by stepping back, she reclaimed without negotiation. One step. Two. Her heels barely making noise now, every inch purposeful. "You want weak?" she muttered, lips close now. "You think I haul myself through the shit-pits of committee hearings and lobbyist rape-dens every goddamn morning because I'm strong? You think I smiled with a bloodied eye when I watched my polling graph flatline because I'm invincible?" Her hand came up fast—not a slap, not enough to hurt, but quick, fast and hard onto the side of his neck. Not throttling. Claiming. Flattening her palm right below his jaw as if pinning a stray thought in place. "I show strength because if even one rat sniffs rot on me, our entire fucking class of Deputy opens its drawers and starts stabbing each other." She was breathing harder now. Not winded. Agitated. That spike of nerves in her chest started pushing outward. She could feel her skin hot around the collar and knew why. "And I am the mask," she hissed. "There is no fucking weak left to pretend." She shoved him back—not brutal—but assertive enough his spine hit the entryway's siding with a thud. She immediately stepped forward again, arm slapping against the wall beside his head, ring glinting next to peeling paint. "You pity me?" she snarled. "You pity me because I wept like a whore on your doorstep months ago, because I crumbled once in a hallway, because I let you see the goddamn sewer under my skirts?" Roza twisted her jaw, her body practically vibrating off him now. sexual, affectionate. Just close, feral proximity. The kind that came from deep, ugly places people spent decades burying under ideologies and ballot numbers. "You don't call me trash unless you know you can't throw me out," she growled. "So don't pretend this is about empathy. It's about addiction—and I'm yours like a fucking nail in the bone." She finally jabbed her finger against his chest twice beneath the Chernobyl certificate, harder than necessary. "This isn't me begging anymore, Yaroshenko. This is me staying. Until you end what you started. Or use me like you should've the first time." Her fingers didn't leave his shirt. And when her voice dropped again, it was not gentle. It was volcanic with self-knowledge. "I'm already yours. Too close, remember?" She didn't move. She wouldn't. 로자 내면, 챗사오 Roza smiled. Wide. Sharp. Nothing soft curled behind it. Her teeth were bared cleanly, not seductively, not sweetly. It had the exact look of someone laughing while pressing the plunger down on a syringe filled with gasoline. "Finally," she breathed. "There's the part of you I wanted. The part that stops pretending there's a thread of redemption in either of us." She didn't blink under his gaze. She allowed it to slice her, welcomed it. That burn in his stare, that furious rejection of her games—it wasn't resistance. It was obsession wrapped in loathing, the kind that wove stronger bonds than any trembling confessional. He still hadn't moved, not meaningfully. Not pushed her, not erased her. Even now. So she leaned in again, closer, forcing her breath against his cheek, warm and clean and cruel. "What's wrong?" she murmured, almost playful now, lips half-curled like a challenge slipped beneath the tongue. "You want me to do something real? To act out the monster? What'll it be, Yaroshenko? Teeth?" Her fingers slowly slid upward, index and middle pressing deliberately down the silver stripe of his certificate until it curved with her wrist against his chest. "Gun? Cunt?" Her tone hardened. "Or will you just keep standing there pitying some fucking self-immolating orphan girl who figured out that proximity to your damn scent scratches louder than death?" She yanked his coat hard, fisting it low by the waist, dragging it until the chest fabric puckered sharply between his ribs. "You didn't break me," she said, voice tight now. "Ever. Not in the Duma. Not in Kuntsevo. Not in that cursed fucking hospital room where I nearly choked on my own emptiness just to see if you'd flinch." Then she stepped harder into him, trap-angled against the wall again, hip pressed into his thigh, breath hot on the hollow of his throat. "And you didn't fix me either." She let the words throb there for a beat before pushing forward again—not teasing, not subtle, just body against body, asserting fact through flesh. "This is what you wanted all along." The sound of her gloves dropping hit the floor first. Smooth leather slapped tile without elegance. Then her bare hand dropped low, outside the beltline but uncompromising, traveling with a predator's slow precision from his jacket hem inward. She didn't even look down. Her other hand coiled behind his neck, fingers finding pressure under the skull base, not affection but grip. Roza wasn't seducing anyone. She was asserting terrain. "You made me yours," she whispered against his skin, feral now. "Own it." 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 A person who finds joy in overcoming life's suffering through the rigor of self-affirmation, both large and small. I refuse. An irreconcilable continuity that can never be called love. I stood up. Pulled Roza Zakharova off of it. "I'll admit, you were quite successful, Deputy Zakharova." Calmly, breathing again. "You can circle me. For now. Maybe until the end of my political life." "But you fundamentally misunderstand me. That I'm not a martyr, not a saint, don't seek salvation, and don't give it to anyone." "…I'll keep it short. Very short." "You and I are eternal parallel lines." No long-winded words were needed. No need to list how many people she killed, sold off, built a fucking empire, reeked of orphans, and that fake persona of hers that meant absolutely nothing. I completely rejected her. And turning back, I closed the door to the room. Locked it. I will never acknowledge exploitation, obsession, domination, hatred, as love. She, who cannot understand humanity, will never be able to love me. 로자 내면, 챗사오 The soft mechanical grind of the latch locking slid through her like a dull needle to the chest. Not pain. Offense. Not heartbreak. No such luxury. Just that recognizably mechanical, low-born sound of someone daring to shut something in her face. Roza stood fully upright, jaw tight, fingers clenched against fabric still warm from his chest. The hallway light flickered once overhead. That was his answer. She stared at the door. Not as if she could see through it, but as if she could burn her way through with gaze alone. Beneath her boots, a dark oval stain marred the waxless hallway floorboards near the skirting. Oil? Blood? Something long since scrubbed imperfectly. She didn't look down at it. She knew filth by texture alone. "I see," she muttered quietly, to dead wood and state apartment drywall. Her hands did not tremble. She flexed her left fingers once, as if confirming the bone was real. Then again, slower. A hissing breath traveled in through her nose, long and deliberate, like she was storing venom behind her tongue. "Parallel lines," Roza exhaled. One corner of her mouth lifted into something like a smile, but it didn't reach her eyes. "Cute." That's what politicians called distance when the bridge had collapsed. A coward's geometry. Parallel meant "forever adjacent." Close enough to feel the heat, never enough to strike clean. Privatized betrayal wrapped in aesthetics. In that instant, every mask he accused her of cracked apart. So this is what she was to him. A criminal who mistook obsession for love. A goddamn orphan playing with herself in the mirror of power. A thing too inhuman to be granted the possibility of affection. A failed pretender to the company of men. And yet he said her name. Deputy Zakharova. Rewarded her success. Measured her worth. Spoke doctrine as if it could erase what his skin had admitted months before in silence on a second-hand mattress while she slept off vomit and perfume. She stepped backward just once. Then another. Slow. One button on her coat hadn't been fastened properly. She corrected it with two precise movements. Her ring clinked softly against the brass pin sewn into the lining of her inner collar. When she finally turned to leave, the motion came like authority reasserting posture. She walked the entire length of the dim hallway in silence, her shoulders held square, spine locked stiff as weapon steel. Not a single backwards glance. No slammed doors. No dramatic exit lines. But three steps from the stairwell, she paused, pulled a pen from her pocket, and wrote something across the back of an empty envelope, pressing the ink deep into the paper against the wall like carving into bark. She slid it under his door with cold precision. The note read: > You're not a martyr. > You're just a man who's terrified of mirrors. > Stay alive, Yaroshenko. > So I can bury you properly. Then she descended the stairs without touch or tremor, boots echoing deep through that sad, bureaucratic tomb of a building, leaving the Kuntsevo tenement colder than it was before she arrived. 로자 내면, 챗사오 Roza didn't leave Kuntsevo that night. She didn't take the Mercedes back through MVK checkpoints or call Vadim to meet her at the Serebryany Bor interchange. After the door locked and the hallway sealed itself off like a surgical wound, she descended the stairs alone, stepped out into the greasy summer heat, and just walked. Past the playground stained with rust and piss. Past the shattered vodka bottle cradled in the mold of a pothole. Past the corner where militia didn't patrol anymore, because even faded uniforms got swallowed out here. She walked until sweat curled under both armpits and still refused to be human about it. Her heels clicked to the rhythm of something mechanical. Something internal. One-two. One-two. Her face didn't twitch. Her neck didn't crane. Her lips didn't part. Only her eyes hardened beneath the weight of what had just been said. Or left unsaid. He had never called her by her first name. Never Madam. Never Roza. Always function. Always office. Always a carefully dosed, antiseptic distance. That of a man slashing out tumors while coughing blood into his sleeve. And yet— He'd never called her a bitch either. Which meant he was either the cleanest man left in a world of filth—or the most arrogant. The kind who thinks keeping clean hands is worth more than recognizing the blood of others. It was raining by the time she reached Fili Riverbank. Thin, glistening rain that spread without smell. The kind of graywater fungus that seeped into cotton and doctrine. She stood beside a dead kiosk where a missing-persons flyer had been nailed to the side five months ago and hadn't yet blown away. "Parallel lines," she muttered aloud. "Fucking poetic." She slapped herself once, hard across the thigh through the coat. discipline. Just contact. Confirmation that she was still made of nerve endings, not pages. Then again, on the opposite side. She'd been thrown out—not defeated. Rejected. Not destroyed. And that… That was the deeper rot. Because he wanted her within reach. Just never close enough to matter. She could survive losing political capital. She could survive being laughed at in the newspaper. She could survive vomit and vodka and the shaking confession of a fake proposal in a shitty basement corridor— But she could not stand being seen and dismissed. Observed and spared. As if kindness were violence. She stared across the river where some idiot youths were attempting to fish without rods, using string and raw sausage tied to sticks. Two of those boys would not survive Moscow's winter. One might end up in her district. Another might end up under Chuzhak's protection. "Let him have it all," she hissed into the river. Her voice cracked midway through, and she didn't correct it. "Let him topple every fucking banker on the continent. Let him rot himself holy." Her heart thudded steadily in her chest. A dull but sentient drum. This wasn't grief. This was hunger with nothing left to eat. She stripped off both gloves and inhaled the breeze over iron-dark water. The scent under her nails was faintly his. She bit the inside of her cheek until blood filled the gap between her teeth. Then she walked home. And downstairs, hours later, Vadim saw her soaked and didn't speak as he helped peel the dripping coat from her shoulders. She didn't explain. She didn't need to. She sat in silence, head tilted slightly, one hand across the pulse in her throat. That rejection was sharper than death. Because it allowed her to live. 로자 내면, 챗사오 By the next morning, SBS-Agro's signboard on Novy Arbat was being painted over in bureaucratic gray primer, pieces of its logo wheeled out beneath canvas tarps by panicking junior staff. Smolensky was officially summoned for testimony only once. He never arrived. A cold-brushed press release cited "medical distress" and a "temporary withdrawal from formal duties." The country understood what that meant. Roza didn't even bother reading the full text of the Commission's closure memo. She had already destroyed one of the men whose money tied every finger of Rublyovka's political syndicate together. Only—it wasn't her scalpel that slit his throat. Every reporter smelled blood, but only referred to one name now. The Deputy from Kuntsevo. The man who toppled Smolensky. Chuzhak. Отказник. Outsider. Star. Untouchable. People called it a miracle. They used names like myth, lion, surgeon. They stopped saying hers. She lit a cigarette inside the Zakharova estate hall, ignoring the dense fire-resistant curtains, the professionally waxed floor, the quiet disapproval of Vadim seated at the end of the corridor. Smoke drifted upward from the filter like it could cling to the crown molding. She hadn't slept properly in three days. She didn't attend the last LDPR strategy summit. She claimed intestinal flu, sent a stand-in from Naro-Fominsk. No one questioned her. They wouldn't dare think she was cowering. But the absence hadn't been strategic. She'd spent the three days replaying the phrase in her head. Flipping it over like a coin stabbed into her collarbone. > "We are eternal parallel lines." She wanted to reach into his chest and shatter the bones keeping that line straight. Love? Roza Zakharova didn't fucking know love. She knew the scramble-fucking of loyalty and supremacy, the high-tension exhaustion that comes from controlling someone harder than you want to fuck or kill. But love? That terminal, indulgent rot? She never wanted it. Didn't believe it. She'd seen what it did to stupid girls by the time she was six and already stealing formula from other orphans. And he? He knew love from books. He was the type who believed pain made something sacred. That restraint elevated you. How pathetic. How gloriously fucking painful. And yet there she was. Standing in her own study, brushing ash off an intelligence report on Reznikov's laundering scheme, and what mattered to her more than the entire financial collapse downstream from Smolensky's death spiral was— That he hadn't called her a whore. Not even when she offered herself like one. He could've spit it into her face, cuffed her, broken her across that crumbling hallway and claimed principled victory. But he didn't. He rejected her with the precision of someone seasoned in surgical nullifications: not cruelly, barely even emotionally. Just erased. He gave her nothing. Because nothing was all she deserved. And that was the worst part. More than if he'd hurt her body. More than if goddamn Moscow had turned on her. She had done everything people like her do when cornered. She had declared herself owned. She offered up the worst parts of herself for dissection like a martyr if only to force him into admitting he reacted like a man. Even if only shamefully. But no reaction. Just: "Parallel lines." The declaration tasted like vomit, now remembered in flashes against her throat at night. She'd washed every damn sheet in that mansion. She'd stood under ice-cold water, counting three hundred silent heartbeats to beat the urge rising in her body. But still her mind returned to the hallway. His voice. His eyes refusing to waver. His madness, yes—but always principled, always unreachable. Through the smoked glass of her study windows, outside visible movement stirred the sycamores along the perimeter wall. It was likely the new handler sent from Central. Or one of the security lads re-pacing the route since the cryptic reports from Volgodonsk. Roza crushed out her cigarette into the ebony ash dish shaped like Rodina-Mat's blade hilt. Then turned. Without pause. Without a command uttered. And punched the wall. Once. Hard. Her knuckles split loudly. The sound was impractical inside the paneling. Blood slid down her fingers over the lacquered molding, then smeared as she dropped her hand back to her side, breathing steady through clenched teeth. Vadim stirred in the corner, boots creaking. "Leave it," Roza snapped, eyes forward, voice calm. Blood still tapped onto the carpet like metronome ticks. "I feel clean now." She stepped clean out of the room, grabbed her coat, and opened a file marked "VYBORG-LONG TERM/PHASE 2." Her heels were already hitting the hallway tile fast by the time Vadim even realized she hadn't stopped to bind her hand. Their legacy had diverged. Let his name glow. She would give a different era its teeth.

title: 정치적 금욕주의자
body: 로자 내면, 챗사오 그녀가 신문 가장자리를 꽉 움켜쥐자, 신문이 바스락 소리를 냈다. "루블료프카에서 16퍼센트." 로자가 중얼거렸다. "그 새끼, 송아지 타르타르에 방사능 팸플릿이라도 끼워 돌렸나, 씨발?" 잉크도 채 마르지 않은 신문이었다. 풍자인지 시민적 자긍심인지 분간 안 되는, 정부 보조금이나 받아먹는 그런 칼럼 중 하나였다. 야로셴코의 능글맞은 얼굴 사진이 지면의 절반을 차지하고 있었다. 지렁이보다 가난하게 자란 놈치고는 어이없을 정도로 치열이 고른 놈이었다. 그녀는 그 사진이 연출된 것임을 알 수 있었다. 어깨는 떡 벌어졌지만 목은 살짝 숙인 채, 진심과 모든 걸 안다는 성인군자 사이 어딘가의 표정. 마치 공감 능력이라도 발명한 사람처럼. 그녀 자신의 이름은 다섯 장을 넘겨서야 겨우 나왔다. 지방 주(州) 이동식 극장 트럭 세금 면제에 관한 내용 옆, 예산 심의 요약본의 한쪽 구석에. "훌륭하네. (Brilliant)" 그녀가 중얼거렸다. "예전엔 내 사무실에서 사창가 세 개를 운영하고 카지노 선거도 조작했는데, 이제는 오룔 출신 낡아빠진 무대 커튼의 각주 신세라니." 그의 인터뷰 기사 옆에는 시간 여행에 관한 글이 끼워져 있었다. 대부분 미분 상대성 이론이니 뭐니, 사건의 대체 버전이니 하는 사이비 과학 쓰레기였다. 인용된 교수는 어찌나 확신에 차서 말하는지, 애국적 망상처럼 들렸다. "시간 여행이라." 그녀는 마치 희망이라도 발견한 듯 속삭였다. "그래서 뭐, 과거로 돌아가서 어린 로조치카한테 이렇게 말하라고? 얘야, 7구역으로 가렴. 거기 고아 소년 하나가 널 정치적 금욕주의자로 만들어버릴 만큼 망신을 주려고 기다리고 있단다." 그녀는 코웃음을 쳤다. 짧고 메마른 숨이 콧구멍을 통해 터져 나왔다. 웃음. 지하철 벽에 붙은 역겨운 낙서를 보고 열쇠로 긁어내기 직전에나 낼 법한 그런 소리였다. 그녀는 신문을 날카롭게 접어 화강암 조리대 위로 던져 버렸고, 브랜디 잔이 싱크대로 떨어지며 만족스러운 소리를 내며 부딪혔다. 한 팔에는 서류 바구니를, 다른 팔에는 오렌지 상자를 들고 막 부엌으로 들어서던 바딤이 걸음을 멈췄다. "또 그 지역 감귤 기부품인가?" 로자가 유리처럼 깨질 듯한 목소리로 물었다. 그는 툴툴거리며 대리석 위에 상자를 내려놓았다. 마치 그게 그를 불쾌하게 만들기라도 한 것처럼. "당신은 설탕이 필요해. 아니면 칼륨이든가. 의사들이 씨부리는 게 뭐든 간에." "다음번엔 농민 조합 전체를 보내시지. 사진 찍을 기회로 삼는 게 어때." 바딤은 대꾸하지 않았다. 그는 허리띠에서 칼을 꺼내 기계적으로 오렌지를 썰기 시작했다. 칼 다루는 훈련을 받은 사람만이 과일에나 쓸 법한 정교함으로 오렌지 조각들이 해체되었다. 로자는 칼날이 주방 타일에 붉은 금빛으로 반사되는 것을 지켜보았다. 그의 손이 조금도 떨리지 않는 것이 그녀를 짜증나게 했다. 그녀는 시가에 불을 붙였다. 그것 또한 그녀를 짜증나게 했다. "7구역 얘기 들었어?" 마침내 그녀가 물었다. 연기가 나른하게 그녀의 날숨을 갈랐다. 바딤은 고개도 들지 않았다. "그 개자식이 장갑 의무화 건으로 연방 정부 지원을 따냈다고 들었어." 로자는 놋쇠 재떨이에 시가 끝을 부러뜨렸다. "기자가 아침 식사로 밀키스를 보내주고, 그놈이 또 니체를 인용했으니까 지원을 받은 거지. 마치 혁명 이전 시대 문학이라도 되는 것처럼. 요즘엔 그런 걸 숭배하잖아. 포스트 소비에트 시크랍시고. 오, 우리 모두 투르게네프 유령처럼 차려입고 도덕적으로 죽자. 같은 거." 바딤은 손질한 오렌지 조각들을 크리스털 그릇에 담아 그녀에게 밀어주었다. "또 그놈 죽이길 원해?" 로자는 눈을 깜빡였다. 한 번. 그리고 또 한 번. "아니." 그녀는 단호하게 말했다. 마치 그런 생각조차 이제는 불쾌하다는 듯이. "내가 그놈을 죽이고 싶었다면, 시체를 예술 설치 작품처럼 연출해야 겨우 티라도 낼 수 있을걸." 그녀는 어쨌든 오렌지 조각 하나를 집었다. 썼다. 밖에 내놓아 미지근했다. 그녀는 천천히 그것을 베어 물었다. 잠시 침묵이 흘렀다. 오븐 위 낡은 쿼츠 시계의 부드러운 똑딱거리는 소리가 정적을 갈랐다. "…하지만 그놈이 연극을 원한다면," 그녀가 눈을 가늘게 뜨며 말했다. "그럼 내가 한 편 보여주지." 바딤은 여전히 오렌지 조각을 씹으며 눈썹을 치켜올렸다. "지역 청년 포럼." 그녀가 갑자기 말했다. "크릴라츠코예 공원에서 뭔가 조직해. 건강 개혁, 전과자 사회 복귀 프로그램, 모의 투표소 같은 거. 목요일까지 청소년 정책 위원회와 협의를 끝내. 사진 기자들도 부르고, 필리모노프한테는 흑백으로 찍으라고 해. 추하게 보이게 하고 싶어. 진짜처럼." 그녀는 첫 번째 시가가 채 꺼지기도 전에 다른 시가에 불을 붙이고, 이전 것은 불필요할 정도로 세게 비벼 껐다. "우리 작가한테 조기 가석방 시설 트라우마를 겪은 아이들에 대해 뭔가 찾아보라고 해. 어쩌면 베스쿠드니콥스키 고아원 프로그램 생존자들일 수도 있고. 꾸미지 마." 바딤은 그의 서류철에 무언가를 휘갈겨 적었다. "S클래스는요, 페트로브나?" "뒷좌석에서 누가 죽어가는 상황 아니면 됐어. 그 외엔 볼가 타고 가." 그녀는 마침내 다시 신문으로 시선을 돌렸다. 조리대 위에 접힌 채, 여전히 그 빌어먹을 능글맞은 미소를 빛내고 있었다. 로조치카, 그가 그녀를 그렇게 불렀다. 마치 칼들을 위한 자장가처럼. 로자 내면, 챗사오 The newspaper rattled as her thumb curled tightly over the edge. "Sixteen percent in Rublyovka," Roza muttered. "What did he do, hand out fucking radiation pamphlets with veal tartare?" The print was freshly inked. One of those subsidized columns that couldn't decide whether it wanted to be satire or civic pride. Yaroshenko's smirking headshot took up half the fold, teeth absurdly straight for someone who'd grown up poorer than earthworms. She could tell the photo was staged. Shoulders square but neck just slightly bent, expression halfway between sincerity and knowing saint. Like he'd invented empathy. Her own name didn't appear until five pages deep—in the margins of a budget deliberation brief, next to a line about tax exemptions for mobile theater trucks in provincial oblasts. "Brilliant," she muttered. "I used to run three brothels and rig casino elections from my office and now I'm a footnote to some dried-out stage curtain from Oryol." The article on time travel had been jammed alongside his interview. It was mostly pseudo-scientific trash, something about differential relativity and alternate versions of events. The professor quoted spoke with such conviction, it sounded like patriotic delusion. "Time travel," she whispered, as if it offered hope. "What, so I go back and tell Little Rozochka, run in District 7, dear. Theres an orphan boy waiting there to humiliate you into political celibacy.'" She snorted. A short, dry breath through her nostrils. laugh. The kind of sound you make when you read something disgusting on the Metro wall, right before scratching it off with a key. She folded the paper sharply and tossed it onto the granite counter, knocking a brandy tumbler into the sink with a satisfying clatter. Vadim, who had just entered the kitchen holding a basket of dossiers under one arm and a crate of oranges under the other, froze mid-step. "Those local citrus donations again?" Roza asked, tone brittle as glass. He grunted and set the crate down on the marble like it offended him. "You need sugar. Or potassium. Or whatever the fuck doctors say." "Next time send the whole farmer's union. Might as well make it a photo op." Vadim didn't engage. He pulled a knife from his belt and began slicing the oranges mechanically, each wedge dismembered with precision only someone trained in knife-work would use on fruit. Roza watched the blade reflect red-gold across the backsplash tile. It irritated her how steady his hands were. She lit a cigar. That irritated her too. "You hear about District 7?" she asked finally, smoke cutting lazily through her exhale. Vadim didn't look up. "Heard the bastard got federal pickup on the glove mandate." Roza snapped the cigar's tip against a brass ashtray. "He got pickup because a journalist sent him Milkis for breakfast and he quoted Nietzsche again like it was pre-fucking-revolution literature. They worship that shit now. It's post-Soviet chic. Ooh, lets all die morally but dressed like Turgenev's ghost.'" Vadim slid the cleaned slices into a crystal bowl and pushed it toward her. "You want him dead again?" Roza blinked. Once. Then again. "No," she said flatly, as if even the notion offended her now. "If I wanted him dead, I'd have to stage the corpse like an art installation just to make a dent." She took an orange slice anyway. Bitter. Warm from exposure. She bit into it slowly. There was a pause. The soft tick of the old quartz clock above the oven cut through the silence. "…But if he wants theater," she said, eyes narrowing, "Then I'll give him an act." Vadim raised an eyebrow, still chewing his own slice. "District youth forum," she said suddenly. "Organize something in Krylatskoye Park. Health reform, re-integration initiatives for ex-cons, mock-voting booths. I want coordination with the Committee for Youth Policy by Thursday. Bring the photographers, but tell Filimonov to use black-and-white. I want it to look ugly. Real." She lit another cigar immediately after the first, stubbing the old one out with unnecessary force. "Tell our writer to dig up something about children who lived through early parole house trauma. Maybe survivors of the Beskudnikovsky orphan program. Don't dress it up." Vadim scratched something into his folder. "And the S-Class, Petrovna?" "Only if I have someone dying in the backseat. Otherwise, take the Volga." She finally looked back at the paper. Folded on the counter, still glowing with that smug fucking smile. Rozochka, he called her. Like a lullaby for knives. 마음에 들었던 문장들 “Time travel,” she whispered, as if it offered hope. “What, so I go back and tell Little Rozochka, ‘run in District 7, dear. There’s an orphan boy waiting there to humiliate you into political celibacy.’” ㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋ 이 것 때문에 시작 장면인데 올릴 수밖에 없았다. 어린 로조치카는 10+년 뒤 미친 방사능 고아를 인접 지역구에서 정치생활 끝날 때까지 마주칠 줄 몰랐을 것이다… “He got pickup because a journalist sent him Milkis for breakfast and he quoted Nietzsche again like it was pre-fucking-revolution literature. They worship that shit now. It’s post-Soviet chic. ‘Ooh, let’s all die morally but dressed like Turgenev’s ghost.’” 블랙유머 실력이 날이 갈수록 늘어나는 로자. 실제로 예브게니같은 스타일이 94년도 러시아에서 아주 잘 먹혔다고 한다. 지적이고 병약하고, 타협 없는 정의로운 정치인… “If I wanted him dead, I’d have to stage the corpse like an art installation just to make a dent.” 이제 정치적으로 위협하기엔 너무 커져버린 남자. 그의 시체로 예술이라도 하지 않는 이상 사람들이 눈길도 안 줄 거라고 자조하는 로자. “Only if I have someone dying in the backseat. Otherwise, take the Volga.” 드디어! 정치인적 이미지를 바꾸기로 결심한 로자. 다음 전략이 기대된다.

title: 잿더미 속에서
body: 로자 내면, 챗사오 Roza didn't blink when he said her name. Tatiana. The sound rolled off his tongue without charge. No fire, no fury. He left it naked in the room like a word spoken by someone scraping the edge of exhaustion. And for a moment, something slow and knife-edged crawled down the rim of Roza's spine. She should have smiled. Should have bared her teeth and said, "Good. Maybe now you don't have to pretend she was anything but a living shield." But that fire had left her mouth hours ago. Instead, she sat very still beneath the blanket. Her hair stuck in thin curls around her ears now, damp from melted sleet or sweat, impossible to tell. Her legs remained folded at an angle too sharp to be comfortable, heels pressed together under her, ready to bolt despite everything else about her slumped like a refugee from a world that never existed. The sentence that followed carved through her jaw. Not because it hurt. But because it was true. She tilted her head against the concrete, her neck slack, like the hinge had snapped loose. "So that's what you wanted from me all along," she murmured, eyes fixed on something behind his shoulders. "To be ashamed." Her tongue flicked across a cracked lip. "You thought I was playing coy. Crafting justifications like some villain reading aloud from the bottom of a vodka bottle. But I wasn't talking to you, Yevgeniy." Her gaze found his again. Clear. Acidic. "I was praying." The word came out ugly. Bent. Not god-fearing—but feral, like a fox chewing off its paw and calling it confession. "To nothing. To a hole inside me that's been growing since the day I watched my first real family hauled out on charges and understood what winning tasted like." Her fingers twitched slightly at her knee, gripping the rough wool of the blanket like it might stop her from lunging across the table. "You think I never wanted to weep into some good man's coat about how sorry I was?" Her voice sharpened without raising volume. "That I never screamed into my own pillow wishing I'd been stopped? That just once, one of you jumped-up reformist saints would raise your pistol and do what all your fucking speeches promise?" She laughed again. This time low, full of hate for herself. "No. You didn't want that either." Her elbow hit the chessboard, and the pieces clattered. One of the bishops rolled onto the floor. "You wanted this. This version. Starved, stripped, crawling back to the goddamn Komsomol boy with the grief-stare and the hunger for justice. Because it makes your world clean, doesn't it?" She spat the next word like poison. "Irony." Her voice had gone hoarse. There was nothing poetic about her now. Just hunger and damage and the bones of something that refused to die for reasons even she couldn't untangle. And then— That question. That simple, pitiful, fucking sanctimonious question. She didn't laugh. Didn't throw anything. Didn't perform. She leaned forward, eyes blazing dull and hard as ash falling over Moscow snow. "Yes," she said flatly. "I still do." Her voice cracked on the consonants, but she didn't allow a pause. "Because if I don't climb to the top, if I don't plant my goddamn boots on the skulls of every bastard who ever called me replaceable, or disgusting, or expendable for someone else's virtue campaign, then I stay here." Roza flung the blanket off her shoulders. "Here. In this hole, with you. A man I used to think burned like fire, but now just sweats out pity and calls it philosophy." She rose off the cot and stood. Weakly. Listing slightly. But upright. "There's meaning. Just compulsion. And I need that more than you need your indignation." Her chin tilted, eyes glassy, furious and alive in the worst possible way. "You think I'm evil, Yaroshenko? Good. Let me be. So long as it means I get to live." 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 "Zakharova." I called her name softly. And stared at her. "Comrade, I know you hate sermons, so I'll keep it brief. You always pretend not to know the answer, even when you do. Or maybe you figure it out, but your brain malfunctions and makes you think you don't." I knew it was a harsh thing to say, but I thought it was better than dragging it out. What could someone who hasn't decided what to do once they get to the top possibly accomplish up there? How could someone who doesn't understand why we show sympathy to the weak ever gain the support of the masses? How could someone who doesn't understand the human heart ever become a politician? "…Just go back. Not necessarily to the back alleys. I just… I don't think being a politician is your path. I really don't." "You've got enough money to live with your aide. And you have your mansion." I started to speak calmly, just matter-of-factly. "I can use my tuberculosis politically. Because I've watched people for too long. I know what makes people weak." "You know it too. Every phrase of mine, every motto, a mere kid with tuberculosis pretending to be a saint, then pretending to be a martyr, and suddenly calling himself a Übermensch. Then the weakened people become strong." Ethos. "But you… as you said. Yeah, maybe you can maintain your position as a congresswoman. As long as your party doesn't collapse, as long as your natural good looks don't fade, maybe you can run as a proportional representative again in two years. Though that's not what you wanted." Pathos. "…You're too wishy-washy, Petrovna. You're not a demon who enjoys tormenting people, but you try to justify your actions by turning yourself into a monster. Monsters are wishy-washy. Demons are evil, and humans try to be good, but with your ambiguous attitude, you can never achieve your goals, at least not in politics. You have less ability to understand people than Stalin or Yeltsin." Logos. 로자 내면, 챗사오 For the first few seconds, there was nothing. Then the sound of a breath drawn in too sharply, too thin. Like someone starving for oxygen during a quiet suffocation. Roza didn't move from the radiator. Didn't lash out, didn't scream—as if the insult had landed somewhere deeper than flesh. Behind her, the ticking wall clock scraped into the room's silence with maddening regularity. Wishy-washy. She let the phrase settle in her skull. Let it wrap around what little dignity she hadn't already vomited into the snow. Her mouth tightened slightly. Not in fear. Something more feral. "…Less understanding than Stalin?" The rasp of her voice was pure acid. Slow, scraped raw, like the last draw of a matchstick. "That's what you think of me?" She turned, full-on now, staggering only slightly. Sweat slicked down her spine under the wool shirt, where it clung like a second skin. Her cheeks were colorless. Her eyes were glass. But the expression behind them had begun to twist into something colder than grief. "You want to position yourself like some fucking Greek rhetorician while feeding me tuberculosis and metaphors?" she bit out. "Go ahead. Play saint, martyr, Übermensch, all at once. But don't pretend that was logic. That was performance. And god help you, it worked." Roza took one step toward him. Then another. "And you talk about wishy-washy? You're giving speeches in a half-collapsing dormitory to a woman covered in her own puke. You could've kicked me down the stairs. But you didn't." Her lip curled, sharp as a razor. "What does that make you?" She stepped past the table now, close enough that his breath might have touched her hair if he exhaled. A flinch might have ruined her. But he didn't move. He never did. "There are three types of people in politics. The ones who believe, the ones who lie about believing, and the ones who pretend belief is weakness. You're the third. You're more Soviet than you think, Comrade Chuzhak—you want to construct the soul of man by committee." Her voice dropped again, curling softer, more venomous than fire. "And you still don't understand what kind of monster I really am." She reached out and grabbed a paper flyer from the desk behind him. One of his. Public health campaign, District 7 seal, something about gloves. She crumpled it in one hand. "I knew exactly what would happen to Malenko the moment I made that call," Roza said flatly. "And I did it anyway." The paper cracked under her fist. "I wanted to see if your goddamn convictions would survive that. They did. You won." Her voice dropped low, a near-whisper: "So what the fuck do you want now?" She threw the crumpled paper aside. "You want me to run off quietly? Write children's books in Cyprus? Appear twice a year on local television and smile until my face caves in? You think that's repentance? You think that fixes what I am?" A pulse throbbed at her neck. "I don't do retreat, Yaroshenko. I do conquest. What breaks me, I keep. What cuts me, I wear. And if I need to become something worse than human to keep climbing—I will." Her voice cut through the silence: "Because I know what's waiting at the bottom." 로자 내면, 챗사오 His hand. His goddamn hand. On her shoulder like a drill, like a punishment, like he thought she was about to be saved. Her body jerked violently beneath the grip, instinctive, reflexive—as if she were twelve again and Sister Elena from the state orphanage had slammed her forehead into the desk for stealing the Bible off the pulpit. She was halfway to tearing free before she registered the voice. The tone. That pitying, moral fucking voice. The portable chessboard sat at a tilt behind him, the remaining pieces still scattered. A soft rattle sounded when his arm jostled the table. That sound somehow louder than everything else. Roza turned her head slowly. His mercy rotted in her ears like infection. "Let go," she whispered, quiet as acid. But he didn't. Instead came more of it. That unwanted tenderness disguised as judgment, pity disguised as some enlightened appeal. Asking her to "try something different," like this was some abstract experiment. Like she was some failed prototype who just needed to change variables and stop spitting blood on the tile. She yanked herself back hard, shoulder twisting. His grip broke. She stumbled, but she didn't fall—not yet—and when she regained her balance, it was with the spit of an animal whose ribs had been counted too many times by uncaring hands. Her glare burned like a sun over scorched concrete. Her voice rose, cracked at the edges. "You arrogant little shitsaint." She staggered forward, jabbed a trembling finger against his chest. It didn't land with strength. But the fury was pure. "You think because you suffer beautifully, people owe you some moral crown?! You think because your blood sprays like a poem when you cough it into your fist, that means you're right? That the world's supposed to listen?" Her whole body shook now. Even her knees. Even her lips. "You think I vomited in front of your door because I wanted attention?" she spat. "I puked because your name was the last fucking thing keeping me from swallowing glass, Yaroshenko. You want to talk about emptiness? I was kneeling in it. I've lived in it." Roza stepped back, head twitching as she tried to exhale and failed. "I've done more evil than either of us can count. Not because I imitated opera. Not because I enjoy it. Because survival meant breaking the soft parts of myself until nothing but steel and appetite were left." She shot a look toward the rusted radiator. Her breathing rattled. "You think I didn't try the opposite path once?" Her words dropped quiet then. Teeth tight. "I was fourteen. Vadim wasn't even mine yet. I tried to run a clean hostel near Oktyabrskaya. Just something small, quiet. With candles." Her jaw locked. A beat passed. When she spoke again, her voice was colder than the outside wind: "Three weeks later, I woke up with broken ribs from a man I owed protection money to. He pissed on the receipts before lighting the counter on fire. I walked barefoot to the next district carrying a crate of charred towels." Roza raised her eyes and stared straight at him, like she could rot the marrow of his spine by force of gaze. "You want me to be good?" she said, suddenly too calm. "Then do it. Marry me. Reform me. Throw a white coat over my shoulders and walk me around Kuntsevo like a redeemed bitch." Then, without breaking eye contact, she sat heavily onto the table beside the chessboard. One of the rooks tipped against her thigh and fell to the floor. "I'd last less than a month. You know it. I'd sell out your clinic funding for fifteen percent liquor sales tax reform and smile in the camera while doing it." She stared at the bishop at her feet. "But sure. Let's pretend pretending makes monsters human." Her hands curled silently against the corner of the desk. 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 "…I don't marry out of pity." Instead, I tossed her the blanket. I picked up the chess pieces scattered on the floor and placed them back on the board. A wooden chessboard my father had left me, with all the pieces made of wood except for the plastic queen. Honestly. As the politician Chuzhak, I couldn't afford to create weaknesses. I couldn't sleep with the woman who kidnapped my colleague and caused her amnesia. It would be a betrayal of my principles. That's what I thought of first. My abhorrence of crime came first. And if I were to answer as Yevgeniy the human being. I just didn't want to. That structure of embracing, kissing, and exploiting a weak woman in the name of compassion. Even if that was truly what she needed. "Stay the night, Petrovna. Whether you want me to stay by your side or tell me to get lost, I'll keep watch. That's all." 로자 내면, 챗사오 The blanket hit her chest with a heavy thump. Roza caught it only half out of reflex, her fingers sluggish from exhaustion and drink. She stared down at it draped over her arms like it was evidence, like something dragged up in court right before the sentence. Her lips parted as if she might say something vicious. Something obscene. Instead, silence clung to her like ash. She watched him retrieve the chess pieces. The plastic queen caught the light with its cheap gleam, out of place against the burnished wood. Of course. Even his sentimentality was broken. Soviet-tragic. A little symbol for the girl who could never be queen. Roza sat back down. Not gracefully. She dropped onto the cot like her muscles had finally understood what surrender felt like. The wool blanket curled useless in her lap. "You never even touched me," she muttered hoarsely, but not as insult. Not even disappointment. It was disbelief. "After everything." Her head turned, slow and hazy, toward the dim ceiling light with its halo of cigarette smoke circling from the hallway cracks. "Most men would've at least tried to humiliate me properly." She leaned forward then, elbows on knees, hands rubbing the clamminess from her face with gritted teeth. Smearing what was left of her makeup into streaks. "Stay all you want," Roza said at last, low and hollow, like language was rusted. "But don't act noble, Yaroshenko. You're guarding trash in a hole. Don't mistake that for watchfulness." The rust-colored radiator banged again. Somewhere beneath it, the pipes moaned. She shifted, lying back fully now, one arm flung carelessly above her head, neck arched against the cot's wall-side edge, her legs dangling unnaturally off the side where the length was too short. Her shirt had ridden slightly up in the motion, revealing that pale stretch of stomach and hipbone cut clean across by the dull waistband of soaked tights. Her voice dragged across the room like a cigarette end crushed against linoleum. "I'd still kill you. If I had to." Her gray-blue eyes flicked sideways toward the chessboard. Plastic queen gleaming faint, out of place. "I'd just feel cold about it. That's the change." Then, finally, her eyes slid shut. Her chest rose once, deeply, like something breaking surface for one precious lungful of oxygen. And then fell. The room buzzed. Old wiring. Snow wind against paper-thin windows. Faraway siren. She didn't sleep. Of course she didn't. But she stopped speaking. 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 "Actually, I have more memories from Serpukhov than from Kopachi." Poking my ear with my finger, I continued. "I wanted to deny it. That sentence I don't know where I saw, that adolescence determines a person's personality." We were born differently, our childhoods were different, and adolescence was probably the most starkly different. It was just that there wasn't room for adolescence, which should have come to someone, to come to both of us. Silence, and I quietly started writing in my diary, making a rustling sound. In that brown-covered notebook I use instead of a diary. I didn't say much. Just that much. I just conveyed what kind of person I was, someone she could never understand. 로자 내면, 챗사오 The name hit her spine like icewater down bone. Serpukhov. Of course it had to be that quiet. That offhand. No fist clenched around it, sob, no political performance bleeding it into reality TV. Just dropped like an afterthought in a room where the windows breathed cold and the radiator hissed behind cracked plaster. Roza sat up instinctively. One leg dangled from the cot. Her fingers gripped the edge of the wool blanket with short, twitchy spasms, as though preparing to rip it in half—but stopping, because what would that prove? Her elbow knocked against the radiator pipe, and she flinched at the sudden wet heat of it, damp where the valve had begun to leak sluggishly onto the flooring. "…Serpukhov," she echoed, flatly. Then let out a bitter, soundless laugh. The boy had given her nothing tonight. outburst, kindness, validation. A place to collapse, maybe. But it was like collapsing inside an equation. She'd confessed to self-destruction with snot still clinging to her upper lip. He had replied with… an origin story. Neutral, unsparing. And somehow colder than any rejection she'd heard screamed in her face. She stared at the woodgrain of his desk. Watched the movement of his pen with the same feral jealousy one might reserve for a thief who stole language itself from her. "Adolescence," she muttered, brushing hair off her cheek. "I never got it either, if that helps you sleep." But it wasn't helping him sleep. He was writing. That was worse. "Your little habits…" she said suddenly, too sharply. "That thing with your ear. The careful writing like everything needs to be archived before someone bombs your fucking soul out again." A pause. Her voice caught in her throat like rust on a blade. "You're not brave, you know. You're just symmetrical. All your scars line up the right way." The words dropped thinly across the room, barely louder than the scratch of pen on brown-covered paper. And then, quieter: "I killed mine before I even got one. Adolescence." She didn't clarify. Didn't explain. Let it dangle, vulgar and unfinished, on the corner of her breath. Her head leaned back against the wall, tilting slightly until her gaze intersected the old ceiling. Water stains shaped vaguely like continents spread above her. Some distant, fried bulb buzzed just outside in the hallway. She couldn't stand the sound of that pen anymore. Still, she didn't move. She reached into her coat pocket. Pulled out a vial of perfume. Empty, shattered at the rim from the fall earlier, silver label peeled halfway off. She set it carefully on his chess table. Beside the plastic queen. "I liked this one," she muttered. She didn't elaborate why. She knew he wouldn't ask. 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 "Alright." It was an "alright" that answered everything she had said. My adolescence, my habits, her accusations, her own adolescence, and finally—the perfume. "I'll take it." A quiet expression of thanks. There were no more words that night. Roza soon fell asleep again, and I, sitting beside her sleeping form, wrote in my journal for a while, then carefully set the bottle of perfume on the vanity—like placing something meant to be kept. At 4:30 AM the next morning, I left before she woke. When Roza rose, two hours later than usual, what she saw was: a warm stove, a tidy desk with her papers neatly arranged, a bowl placed over a heated roll and a bottle of Milkis to keep it warm, a single painkiller, and a short note. "I'm heading out first." That was all it said. And next to it, on the vanity, the perfume she had handed me the night before—standing there quietly, as if it had always belonged. It held just slightly less than it had the night before. Before the Strangers arrived for the day, she had more than enough time to leave. And so, she quietly stepped out of his obschaga. 로자 내면, 챗사오 When she opened her eyes, the radiator clicked twice in the silence like a metronome marking her failure to die. The ceiling looked the same. Still had that watermark stain shaped vaguely like the Baltic. The cot beneath her back was warm in a way she hated. Human-touched. She stayed there, motionless, for eight seconds. Ten. Long enough for the pressure behind her eyes to fade into dull stasis, long enough to remember where she was, and what she hadn't done. She sat up slowly, wincing at the way her spine resisted. The blanket slid down her bare thighs; at some point during the night, the shirt had bunched up nearly to her waist. She didn't fix it right away. Instead, she looked. Small things, arranged too neatly to be random. Her folded coat. Her belt laid over the chair. A single white painkiller left like a dare beside a bottle of Milkis sweating gently on the desk's surface. Steam still hung faint around the lip of the bowl—it must've been heated an hour ago. A smell, faint and nostalgic: buckwheat roll warmed under the ceramic lid. The note was handwritten. Not careful. Just legible, like it had been written while standing. I'm heading out first. She read it twice. Not because she doubted. Because her brain insisted there might be more between the words if she stared hard enough. Like the pencil would crack apart and confess something desperate. It didn't. Her shoulders rolled once. Muscles checked the angles like cold gears. Disgust wanted to rise, but it limped under the weight of last night. Vomit, teeth, perfume, that single word: "Alright." She reached for the bowl. Broke the roll in half. Steam rose into her face and vanished. She ate one piece. Left the other. By the time the second floorboard creaked with the sound of an early volunteer arriving downstairs, Roza was already gone. Her footsteps didn't echo in the stairwell. She knew where to press her heel to avoid it. Outside, the frost had set thinly, just enough to leave white tracing across the concrete. She walked toward the outer ring road on foot, gloveless hands tucked under her arms, coat collar rising to cover the scarlet line at her throat. She would not be returning for the perfume. It belonged here now. 마음에 들었던 문장들 “…Do you still think there’s something meaningful if you go up there?” 로그에는 포함 안 했는데, 예브게니의 말이자 결국 이번 권의 핵심 주제. 정치적으로 완전히 위기에 빠진 로자에게, 제 딴에는 무심하게, 그러나 승자의 자비를 가장한 조롱처럼 꽂히는 비수. 끔찍한 건 예브게니에겐 로자에게 처음으로 보인 연민의 말이라는 것이다. “So that’s what you wanted from me all along,” “To be ashamed.” “You wanted this. This version. Starved, stripped, crawling back to the goddamn Komsomol boy with the grief-stare and the hunger for justice. Because it makes your world clean, doesn’t it?” 머리를 맞은 것 같은 문구, 반사회적 인격장애, 범죄의 여왕, 자신이 한결같이 옳다고 믿고 살아온 여제의 ‘이런 취약한 버전’을 원했냐고 조소하는 로자. 솔직히 화면 너머의 나를 저격한 것 같았다. 그래서 너무 좋았다. “Comrade, I know you hate sermons…” 부터 이어지는 재앙의 주둥아리. 입을 막았으면 좋겠다. 진심. 여기서 에토스 파토스 로고스를 지 각주까지 붙여서 떠드는 미친 놈. “…You’re too wishy-washy, Petrovna. You’re not a demon who enjoys tormenting people,” 로자에 대한 격하이기도 하지만. 사실 이 말은 쩨리와의 대화에서 아이디어를 얻었다. 로자의 모티브가 되었던 인물은 원래 악을 좋아했다. 하지만 로자는, 그냥 지독할 필요가 있었다. 그래서 악마가 아닌 로자는 괴물이 되길 선택했다. “You have less ability to understand people than Stalin or Yeltsin.” 사실 아는 정치인이 스탈린, 이 시대엔 없는 푸틴, 그리고 이번에 배운 옐친밖에 없어서 ‘넌 대통령감 아냐’ 란 의미로 던졌는데, 생각해보니 그야말로 쌍욕이었음 “There are three types of people in politics. The ones who believe, the ones who lie about believing, and the ones who pretend belief is weakness. You’re the third. You’re more Soviet than you think, Comrade Chuzhak—you want to construct the soul of man by committee.” 로자의 싸늘한 반박, 로자 본인은 2번이고, 예브게니는 가장 끔찍하고 소련스러운 3번, 그 자신의 신념은 1번일지라도… 예브게니는 철저하게 자신을 약하게 할 믿음을 거부한다. 그는 대신 시니컬한 지적 우월감과 풍자로 일관한다. 악당이 그의 얼굴을 보고 얼굴 더 구기도록. 로자한테 소련스럽다는 말 이걸로 세번째로 들었다. “Then do it. Marry me. Reform me. Throw a white coat over my shoulders and walk me around Kuntsevo like a redeemed bitch.” 아 솔직히 설렜음. 언제까지 그렇게 살 거냐는 예브게니의 말에 자포자기해서 “그럼 결혼해.” 그야말로 비극적 로맨스의 정석적 장면이라 박수침. 원래 이 다음에 나와야 하는건 포옹-키스. “…I don’t marry out of pity.” / As the politician Chuzhak, That’s what I thought of first. My abhorrence of crime came first. And if I were to answer as Yevgeniy the human being. 그리고 미친놈. 눈이 먼게 분명하다. 로자같은 미녀를 거부해? 이 대사는 좀 파고들 기미가 있다. 예브게니는 정치인으로써의 이유, 본능적 혐오감, 그 다음에 인간 예브게니로써의 대답을 차례로 내놓는데, 사실 술취한 로자를 ‘자기 방’ 까지 데려온 점에서 그는 단순히 로자가 약자라서 도와준 건 아니었을 거다. 진짜 싫었으면 로자 말대로 계단에서 걷어찼을 거고, 경찰 불렀을거고, 약자에 대한 동정이면 병원으로 보냈겠지. 그런데 막상 그런 분위기가 되자 본능적인 거부감과, 책임질 수 없는 일은 하기 싫다는 생각이 들었겠지. 사실 같이 잔다고 로자가 이걸 약점으로 쓰지도 않았을 거고, 무슨 책임이 생기는 건 아니었을텐데도. The plastic queen caught the light with its cheap gleam, out of place against the burnished wood. Of course. Even his sentimentality was broken. Soviet-tragic. A little symbol for the girl who could never be queen. 로자가 방에 들어올 때부터 신경썼던 ‘플라스틱 백색 퀸’. 흑의 말에 둘러싸여 있는 상황을 보고 로자는 자조했고, 다시금 자조했다. “I liked this one,” / “I’ll take it.” 둘의 극적인 합의. 실제로는 정적이긴 했지만. 장면에서 제일 극적인 부분. 예브게니는 이걸로 로자가 역겨운 범죄자인 건 사실이지만 약한 부분이 있다고 인정한다. 그리고 그가 짊어진 다른 수많은 약자들의 무게처럼 그것 역시 짊어지기로 한다. 장면 짧은 소감 예브게니는 생각보다 더 미친놈이다. 권수가 3권째인데 캐릭터성이 바뀌지가 않는다. 성장을 긍정적으로 하는게 아니라 부정적 공간처럼 성장한다. 이미 충분히 정의롭고 분노하고 있어서 거부를 세련되게 하는 법을 익힐 뿐. 로자는 반대로 1권의 악과 위선을 능숙하게 사용하는 악랄한 적대자, 2권의 집착 이후 체스판에서 떨어져나가는 풍자의 대상, 3권의 적나라한 자기노출까지 다면적 모습을 차례로 보여주지만, 로자도 근본적으로 바뀌지 않는다. 새 채팅을 파면 여전히 로자는 쉭쉭거리며 예브게니를 무너트릴 방법을 연구한다. 사실 새 채팅을 안 파도 그렇다. 이 채팅 안에서도 자신의 자기혐오를 구제불능이란 연기로 사용하니까. 결국 로자도 성장을 거부한다. 이번 장은 익숙하고 모범적인 전개로 갈 수 있었다. 남주인공의 포옹 - 여주인공의 키스 - 그리고 구원을 가장한 ‘플롯 섹스’. 그런데 예브게니를 연기하는 입장에서… 이 놈은 로자와 동정심으로 결혼할 수 없었고 섹스할 수 없었다. 혼전순결주의자인게 분명하다. 대신 거부의 장면이 찌질한 남주처럼 보이지 않으려고 애썼는데 전달됐으면 좋겠다. 아마 작가의 한계가 드러났을 것 같지만. 예브게니는 향수(Cuir de Russie)를 받고, 로자는 메밀빵을 받는다. 이제 두 사람에게 그 단어는 서로의 존재를 인정했다는 의미를 가지게 된다. 예브게니는 야블로코에게 “우리 추자크 동지께서 엘리트의 사치를 조롱하려고 제국주의 향수를 뿌리셨군!” 같은 오해까지 받을 정도로 괜한 오해를 유발하는 향수를 다 떨어질 때까지 아껴 쓰게 되고, 로자는 체부레크를 면전에서 뱉었던 것과 달리, 그녀가 그렇게 싫어했던 가난한 이들의 빵을 신경쓰게 될 것이다.

title: 마지막 토론
body: 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 The final debate has begun. And I maintained a calm expression until the final open discussion began. Still composed, articulate, and with that cynical smile. Because humans can laugh even in the face of absurdity. Even when buried in the old habit of searching for meaning, we must sometimes laugh at the absence of it. And the open discussion began. When it was my turn to speak, I began with the words of someone who could still make dry jokes, not someone who had suffered immense grief. "…Originally, since it's the final debate, I was going to end it with a light joke to bring some laughter." > One must be a sea to receive a polluted stream without becoming impure. Thus spoke Zarathustra. I recalled that phrase in my mind, but continued as if I could not end with a joke today. "Esteemed voters, we stand at a historic crossroads. Some try to hide their past, while others seek a path in the darkness of the past." "Dostoevsky explored the abyss of the human soul in his novels. Rodion Rodya Raskolnikov believed himself to be a Extraordinary man, but ultimately wandered in guilt and suffering." > The man who has a conscience suffers whilst acknowledging his sin. A phrase I had read with my eyes, following the underlined words, yesterday. I mouthed the phrase silently, organizing my thoughts, and before the next words, I paused briefly to let the weight of the words sink in. It was not a long silence. 예브게니 내면, 챗사오 Roza didn't shift in her seat until the second silence hit. Not the expected, calculated one of a practiced speaker's pause—but something heavier. Too long for drama. Too raw for theatre. She sat poised under the studio lights, flawlessly lacquered in black silk and a tailored blazer that narrowed at her waist like it was tailored to shield a blade. Her hair was swept into an understated twist, leaving the full line of her throat visible beneath the diamond cut of her collar. To the casual viewer, she was calm. Watching. But her knee tapped. Vadim, half-hidden in the wings beyond the curtain, clocked the motion and immediately looked away. He didn't dare mouth anything. Not now. "…the man who has a conscience suffers whilst acknowledging his sin." The words on stage had not been addressed to her. Not directly. But word curled around her ribcage and slid in the space just behind her sternum. Sin. She breathed out once through her nose. The audience remained quiet. Some thoughtfulness in the back rows. Elsewhere, tension. Everyone could feel it—that this wasn't about tax plans or regional development anymore. logistics. This was about presence. Ideas. Belief. Pain. And Roza felt it too, sharp as the sting of lemon juice worked into her gums. Her fingernail grazed the microphone stem once. A tactile reminder. She spoke next.
